t: You cannot make vitamin C. Nor can a chimp, or a guinea pig. A dog can. The recipe is in you — it is just broken.
You carry the gene for making vitamin C. So do chimps and guinea pigs. In all of you it is broken, which is why you need fruit — and a dog, whose copy works, does not.
sub: Why would anyone be given a recipe that does not work?
The interesting question is not the missing ability. It is the presence of the broken instructions for it.

question: Two children hand in the same essay with the same spelling mistake in the same word. What do you think?
Two pupils submit essays containing an identical, unusual error in the identical place. What is the natural conclusion?
options: One copied the other, or both copied something else
They both happened to make the same mistake
The mistake proves nothing at all
stages.outcome: One copied the other, or both copied something else
note: Commit. Note that shared correctness proves nothing here — everyone spells common words the same. It is the shared error that carries the weight.

t: When the same broken bit turns up in the same place in two creatures, that is called a shared error.
Identical damage at an identical position in two genomes is a shared error — and it is treated very differently from shared function.
Shared derived defects: pseudogenes disabled by the same lesion at the same nucleotide, and endogenous retroviral insertions at the same genomic coordinate in different species.

The argument turns on the vast size of the space of possible errors. Function can be independently arrived at; a specific inactivating mutation at a specific site, or a viral insertion at one of billions of possible loci, cannot easily be.
sub: There are millions of ways to break something. Breaking it the same way twice by accident is very unlucky.
Working parts can match because both work. Broken parts matching in the same way is a much narrower coincidence.
Humans and chimps share thousands of endogenous retroviral insertions at matching loci, and the vitamin C pseudogene is disabled by the same deletion in both.
Roughly 8% of the human genome is retroviral in origin, and the insertion sites are shared with other primates in a nested pattern that matches the tree derived from anatomy.

t: The broken genes are really there, in the same places. Here is what each side makes of that.
The sequence data are not in dispute. What they license is.
evidence: The same broken vitamin C recipe sits in the same place in humans and chimps, damaged the same way. Thousands of old virus insertions line up too.

The GULO pseudogene is inactivated by shared lesions across primates; thousands of endogenous retroviral insertions occupy matching genomic coordinates; and independent gene sets recover largely congruent nested trees.

claim: The same breaks are in the same places because they were inherited from a shared ancestor.
Shared derived defects are inherited: the damage happened once, in an ancestor, and everything descended from it carries the same scar.
because: There are millions of ways to break a gene. Two creatures breaking it identically by chance would be an enormous coincidence — but inheriting one old break is ordinary.

The pattern is nested and congruent across independent character sets — anatomy, several unlinked gene families, retroviral insertion sites, and developmental sequence — which is a far stronger claim than resemblance. Statistically, the probability of independent identical insertion at matching loci thousands of times over is vanishing.
predicts: New genes should keep giving the same family tree as the old ones.
Newly sequenced genomes should fall into the existing nested hierarchy, and newly examined pseudogenes should show damage shared exactly along the tree and not across it.

claim: Similar creatures were built to a similar plan, and some of those broken bits are not really broken.
Sequence similarity reflects common design; and much of what was called junk or broken has since been found to do something.
because: The same designer using the same plan explains the matching. And things called useless before have turned out to have a job — so calling something broken may just mean we have not found out what it does.

They point to the substantial functional roles now assigned to non-coding DNA and to some endogenous retroviral sequences — some are co-opted in placental development — and argue the 'shared mistake' framing assumes non-function it cannot demonstrate. They also press cases where gene trees conflict with one another and with anatomy.
predicts: More of the 'broken' parts should turn out to have jobs.
Continued discovery of function in sequences currently classed as degraded, and continued discordance between trees built from different genes.

ask: If a broken part turned out to have a job, would that settle it? What if it did not?

Test the reasoning on both sides. Does discovering a function for some retroviral insertions bear on why the insertion sites match position-for-position? And does congruence across gene trees follow from design, or is it compatible with any nested arrangement a designer chose? Ask each account what result it would count as a loss.

q: Why do scientists care more about shared mistakes than shared working parts?
Why is a shared defect treated as stronger evidence than a shared function?
Why does a shared inactivating lesion carry more inferential weight than shared function?
options: Because there are far more ways to break something than to make it work
Because broken things are more interesting
Because working parts are harder to compare
why: Two people can spell a word right for the same reason: it is right. Spelling it wrong the same way needs an explanation.

Function constrains: there may be only a few ways to build a working enzyme, so independent arrival at the same solution is unremarkable. Failure does not constrain — the space of possible breaks is huge, so a shared specific break is a much narrower coincidence.

It is an argument from the size of the outcome space. Convergence on function is expected under constraint; convergence on one particular lesion out of an enormous set of equally-disabling alternatives is not. This is why the argument targets shared derived defects specifically, and why demonstrating function in the sequence is the relevant counter-move.

t: This is how they work out where a new virus came from, in days.

Comparing sequences to build trees is routine public-health infrastructure: tracing a new outbreak to its source animal and tracking variants through a population both run on exactly this method, on a timescale of days.
